Ibidunmoye, Hernandez-Rodriguez and Elmroth (2015). Performance Anomaly Detection and Bottleneck Identification. ACM Computing Surveys.
https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2%3A839537/FULLTEXT01.pdf
Surveys performance anomaly detection and bottleneck analysis.
Supports telemetry analysis; does not validate ARQ thresholds.
Liu, Ting and Zhou (2008). Isolation Forest. ICDM.
https://www.lamda.nju.edu.cn/publication/icdm08b.pdf
Uses isolation trees to score unusual observations.
Standard model baseline; ARQ evaluates it and a support-aware candidate separately from bracketed recovery.
Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997). Long Short-Term Memory. Neural Computation.
Introduces recurrent modeling of temporal dependencies.
Background only; no trained LSTM is established here.
Malhotra et al. (2016). LSTM-based Encoder-Decoder for Multi-sensor Anomaly Detection.
https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00148
Detects unusual sequences through reconstruction error.
Sequence reconstruction is prior work, not a new ARQ mechanism.
Lo et al. (2016). Improving Resource Efficiency at Scale with Heracles. ACM TOCS.
https://research.google/pubs/improving-resource-efficiency-at-scale-with-heracles/
Manages colocated resources with feedback to protect latency.
Latency-driven allocation and recovery are established.
Fried et al. (2020). Caladan: Mitigating Interference at Microsecond Timescales. OSDI.
https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/fried
Uses fast allocation and contention signals for isolation.
ARQ does not reproduce its scheduler or timing scale.
Chen, Delimitrou and Martinez (2019). PARTIES: QoS-Aware Resource Partitioning for Multiple Interactive Services. ASPLOS.
https://www.csl.cornell.edu/~martinez/doc/asplos19.pdf
Dynamically partitions resources for colocated interactive services.
Multi-service QoS feedback is not novel to this project.
Ousterhout et al. (2019). Shenango: Achieving High CPU Efficiency for Latency-sensitive Datacenter Workloads. NSDI.
https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi19/presentation/ousterhout
Adjusts CPU allocations to changing service demands.
Provides a scheduling comparison, not an ARQ implementation.
Zhang et al. (2013). CPI2: CPU performance isolation for shared compute clusters. EuroSys.
https://research.google/pubs/cpi2-cpu-performance-isolation-for-shared-compute-clusters/
Uses CPI observations to identify interference and throttle likely offenders.
Interference-aware selective throttling already exists.
Delimitrou and Kozyrakis (2014). Quasar: Resource-Efficient and QoS-Aware Cluster Management. ASPLOS.
https://csl.stanford.edu/~christos/publications/2014.quasar.asplos.pdf
Combines classification with resource allocation and assignment.
Learned resource decisions are established research.
Delimitrou and Kozyrakis (2013). Paragon: QoS-aware scheduling for heterogeneous datacenters. ASPLOS.
https://mast.stanford.edu/pubs/paragon_qos_aware_scheduling_for_heterogeneous_datacenters/
Accounts for hardware heterogeneity and workload interference.
A broader placement problem than local CPU-quarantine release.
Mars et al. (2011). Bubble-Up: Increasing Utilization In Modern Warehouse Scale Computers Via Sensible Co-Locations. MICRO.
https://research.google/pubs/bubble-up-increasing-utilization-in-modern-warehouse-scale-computers-via-sensible-co-locations/
Applies tunable memory pressure to characterize interference sensitivity.
Active perturbation for interference assessment is known.
Banga, Druschel and Mogul (1999). Resource Containers: A New Facility for Resource Management in Server Systems. OSDI.
https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi-99/presentation/resource-containers-new-facility-resource-management-server-systems
Separates resource accounting principals from protection domains.
Resource management and security isolation are distinct.
Hindman et al. (2011). Mesos: A Platform for Fine-Grained Resource Sharing in the Data Center. NSDI.
https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi11/mesos-platform-fine-grained-resource-sharing-data-center
Coordinates fine-grained sharing across cluster frameworks.
Cluster allocation differs from this local recovery experiment.
Verma et al. (2015). Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg. EuroSys.
https://research.google/pubs/large-scale-cluster-management-at-google-with-borg/
Describes large-scale workload placement and cluster management.
Deployment scale and guarantees are not comparable to ARQ.
Schwarzkopf et al. (2013). Omega: flexible, scalable schedulers for large compute clusters. EuroSys.
https://research.google/pubs/omega-flexible-scalable-schedulers-for-large-compute-clusters/
Uses shared state and optimistic concurrency for scheduling.
Does not establish this prototype as a cluster scheduler.
Ghodsi et al. (2011). Dominant Resource Fairness: Fair Allocation of Multiple Resource Types. NSDI.
https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi11/dominant-resource-fairness-fair-allocation-multiple-resource-types
Defines multi-resource fair allocation.
ARQ does not implement DRF or prove allocation fairness.
Rzadca et al. (2020). Autopilot: Workload Autoscaling at Google Scale. EuroSys.
https://research.google/pubs/autopilot-workload-autoscaling-at-google-scale/
Automates resource sizing and scaling for workloads.
Autoscaling evidence cannot be transferred to ARQ.
Kulkarni et al. (2019). Pliant: Leveraging Approximation to Improve Datacenter Resource Efficiency. HPCA.
https://www.csl.cornell.edu/~nsk49/publication/pliant_hpca/
Uses approximation to reduce colocation contention.
ARQ changes CPU duty, not application approximation quality.
Belay et al. (2012). Dune: Safe User-level Access to Privileged CPU Features. OSDI.
https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi12/technical-sessions/presentation/belay
Exposes privileged CPU facilities safely to a Linux process using virtualization hardware.
ARQ uses ordinary process controls; it does not implement Dune or hardware-backed isolation.
Kaffes et al. (2019). Shinjuku: Preemptive Scheduling for Microsecond-scale Tail Latency. NSDI.
https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi19/presentation/kaffes
Uses fine-grained preemption to reduce head-of-line blocking across variable-length requests.
Scheduling latency is established prior work. ARQ has no comparable microsecond scheduler.
Cho et al. (2020). Overload Control for Microsecond-scale RPCs with Breakwater. OSDI.
https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/cho
Uses queue-delay-driven admission credits, demand speculation and overload handling.
Increasing a grant to expose unmet demand has conceptual overlap; admission credits differ from CPU-duty relaxation.
Qiu et al. (2020). FIRM: An Intelligent Fine-grained Resource Management Framework for SLO-Oriented Microservices. OSDI.
https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/qiu
Uses telemetry and machine learning to localize contention and adapt resource provisioning.
ML-assisted SLO control is established. ARQ must justify its particular recovery protocol rather than claim ML control generally.
Zhang et al. (2021). Sinan: Data-Driven, QoS-Aware Cluster Management for Microservices. arXiv:2105.13424.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.13424
Models microservice dependencies to allocate resources while protecting end-to-end tail latency.
ARQ does not model a microservice dependency graph or validate comparable end-to-end QoS.
Gan et al. (2021). Sage: Leveraging ML to Diagnose Unpredictable Performance in Cloud Microservices. arXiv:2112.06263.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.06263
Uses unsupervised models for online root-cause diagnosis and corrective performance actions.
Root-cause inference and correction are known; ARQ gate outcomes do not identify a unique cause.
